extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors and educators looking for resources on teaching and assessing mathematical writing and communication
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of instructor-facing resources, rubrics, checklists, and classroom activities for teaching, assessing, and improving mathematical writing, proofs, and presentations in undergraduate courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric for Problem of the Week
rubrics_metrics.description: Janet Preston at Unity College uses the rubric attached below to grade short writing assignments; the rubric is based on one she saw at mathforum.org. At Unity College, we have adopted a college-wide goal to incorporate writing across the curriculum. To bring a writing component into our classes, my math colleagues and I use writing assignments like the weekly problems provided at mathforum.org. The way it works is this: Every two or three weeks throughout the semester, I choose a problem or project, relevant to our topic at hand, that I think will...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: rubric used to grade short writing assignments as part of a regular 'Problem of the Week' (chosen every 2–3 weeks) to integrate writing across the curriculum. Based on a mathforum.org rubric; intended to provide a practical grading tool for frequent, short assignments. (Full rubric appears attached on the original post.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments codes for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: This list of common comments on mathematics papers, with comment codes, can be used to avoid rewriting the same comment on several papers. The codes are useful for de-emphasizing less important comments so students will focus on more important written-out comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes Tex and doc files for modification and copy/paste onto student papers. Intended for short papers; a separate list would be needed for longer papers with more structure-focused comments. ‘Grader’ versions are designed to help educators quickly skim to find the code for a desired comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: This revision checklist was written for MIT’s Project Laboratory in Mathematics in the Spring of 2014, to provide students with strategies for revising their research paper drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus: practical strategies for revising research-paper drafts; intended as a step-by-step checklist students can use during revision. (Authored by Susan Ruff and David Jerison.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of Effective Communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples contrasting two student presentations: Johann’s presentation was mathematically correct, neat and legible board work, professional delivery, perfect timing, but dry and failed to engage; Karen’s presentation gained and held attention and successfully conveyed the beauty and power of generating functions to part of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit evaluative criteria: mathematical correctness; neat, legible board work; professional delivery; appropriate timing; ability to gain and hold audience attention; ability to convey the conceptual ‘beauty and power’ of the mathematics; audibility and reach (ensuring the whole class can hear/understand). Usefulness: highlights that technical correctness alone is insufficient—engagement and communication clarity matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-scrambling activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must correctly order the scrambled sentences of a proof. These activities help students identify when a proof is logically correct, to recognize how authors use words like 'therefore,' 'next,' etc., to indicate the direction of the logic, and to gain experience reading and comprehending proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials enclosed include two activities, a quiz, and notes for educators. Pedagogical goal: train students to recognize logical flow and discourse markers in proofs; diagnose understanding of proof structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: On teaching math communication
rubrics_metrics.description: An 18‑page resource for math instructors addressing questions of how to teach communication in an undergraduate math seminar. Most of the document focuses on questions of grading and providing feedback to students on their writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written for a workshop with MIT math instructors preparing to teach communication-intensive undergraduate math seminars; practical guidance on grading policies, feedback strategies, and course design for communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum Overhang – annotated
rubrics_metrics.description: The article 'Maximum Overhang' (by Paterson et al.) is annotated to point out to students how to write a mathematics paper. The annotations address the structure and content of an introduction, how to integrate equations, text, and figures, how to guide the audience through the content, how to cite, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an award-winning published article as a model; annotations highlight concrete writing practices: structuring an introduction, integrating math and exposition, using figures effectively, guiding reader flow, and citation practices. Serves as a sample and teaching tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing workshop questions for students
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-page reading assignment that presents questions for students to consider as they read a draft of one of their instructor’s published papers. This assignment precedes a workshop on how to write a paper, in which the students discuss the draft and a revised version of the paper as well as writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: priming students to critique and learn from a published draft before participating in a workshop; encourages reflection on structure, clarity, and revision choices. From Pedro Reis’ Undergraduate Seminar in Physical Applied Mathematics at MIT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing a term paper
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief handout providing advice for the process of writing a term paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical process-oriented advice for students writing a term paper; from Olivier Bernardi’s Undergraduate Seminar in Discrete Mathematics. Likely covers topic selection, drafting, revision, and organization (full content on the original post).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two proof variants (discussion of elegance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two proofs of the identity 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 (one by induction; one by pairing terms) used to start a class discussion about elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical goal: compare proof techniques and discuss criteria of elegance in mathematical argument (brevity, insight, structure). Use concrete example proofs to stimulate discussion about proof quality beyond correctness.
